newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, Turkmenistan hope to start on pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, Turkmenistan hope to start on pipeline.

text.p: Pakistan and Turkmenistan plan to start building a $2.5 billion-gas pipeline across war-ravaged Afghanistan this year, a government minister said on Friday.

Pakistan's Petroleum and Natural Resources Minister Nisar Ali Khan told a news conference it would then take two years to complete the pipeline, designed to carry 20 billion cubic metres of gas a year from Turkmenistan to Pakistan.
Khan said Pakistan planned to intensify efforts to promote stability in Afghanistan to enable the gas project and others to go ahead.
Leaders of warring Afghan factions and "relevant countries" -- Iran, Tajikistan, Turkey, Uzbekistan -- would be invited for peace talks in Pakistan, he said, but gave no date.

He said the heads of government of Pakistan and Turkmenistan had signed a protocol setting out a schedule for work to start on the pipeline, due to terminate in the Pakistani city of Multan, with an option to extend it to a third country.

Under the agreement signed this week on the sidelines of a summit of the 10-nation Economic Cooperation Organisation in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat, the two countries decided to set up a task force to hammer out financial and technical aspects.
"They are going to meet in the first week of June in Islamabad and again by the end of June in Ashgabat," Khan said.
In the meantime, discussions would continue on the formation of a consortium to undertake the project.
"We hope that by October, all the aspects, all the problems, will be sorted out and work on the project should start before the end of the year," Khan said.

He said the U.S. oil firm Unocal had been included in the Pakistan-Turkmenistan agreement because Ashgabat wanted Unocal to build the pipeline. An Argentine company, Bridas, is also competing for the project.

A Taleban leader said in Kabul this week that the purist Islamic movement, which holds most of Afghanistan, would sign a deal with whichever company "can give us more advantages and who will sooner start their work".
Khan said agreement had also been reached on building an oil pipeline from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan to Pasni on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast and an oil terminal.
The project would cost $2.0 billion and take 18 months to complete once construction begins. Pakistan would buy some of the oil and the rest could be exported, Khan said.
Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, seeking new outlets for their oil, had also agreed to join the project.

"A very minor extension will enable the Kazakhs and the Uzbeks to put their oil in this pipeline, and the actual pipeline would be (through) Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan," he said.
Khan said Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif had met ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani in Ashgabat and assured him the new Pakistani government was not taking sides in Afghanistan.
Khan said the gas and pipeline projects could begin even in the absence of an overall Afghan settlement because their routes lay through territory controlled by the Islamic Taleban militia.
The Taleban, accused by its opponents of being a creation of Pakistan, captured the capital Kabul in September but have yet to win international recognition.
Khan acknowledged that financing the pipeline projects might be difficult as long as the Afghan conflict continued.
